planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown in fall or early spring; give a sturdy structure to climb since canes can reach 15-20 ft.

directions: Train this vigorous climbing tea-noisette along a fence, arbor, or wall with horizontal support to encourage lateral flowering shoots. Blooms are large, quartered, and buff-apricot with a rich tea fragrance, appearing in flushes from spring through fall in warm climates. It tolerates heat and humidity well, making it a long-time favorite in southern gardens, but benefits from good air circulation to deter blackspot. Prune lightly after the first flush to shape and remove spent wood, saving hard pruning for late winter dormancy.

planting.note: Best planted as a climbing structure specimen; give it a trellis or pillar since it is more shrubby than other noisettes.

directions: This noisette produces clusters of small, cupped, apricot-orange blooms that fade to buff-yellow as they age, set against glossy dark foliage. It flowers in repeated flushes through the growing season and performs reliably in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast where many hybrid teas struggle. Give it light support as a pillar rose or let it sprawl as a large shrub. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering and watch for blackspot in wet years.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, full-sun bed; mulch heavily in zone 7 and colder.

directions: Anna Olivier bears long, elegant buds that open to blush-buff double blooms often tinged with rose-pink at the petal edges, carried on a graceful, almost willowy bush. Like most tea roses, it blooms continuously through heat and humidity where hybrid teas falter, making it a standby for Deep South gardens. Light, frequent pruning keeps the naturally twiggy growth tidy, and good drainage prevents root problems in heavy soils. Fragrance is mild to moderate with a classic tea-rose note.

planting.note: Choose a full-sun site with good drainage; this tea is more compact than many of its class.

directions: This compact tea rose produces velvety, deep maroon-red double blooms with a strong, sweet tea fragrance that intensifies in warm weather. It is a reliable repeat bloomer in Gulf Coast conditions and generally more resistant to fading in intense sun than other dark red roses. Keep it on the drier side once established, since tea roses dislike soggy feet, and prune lightly through the season to maintain a compact, bushy habit. Watch for blackspot in humid summers and thin congested canes for airflow.

planting.note: Best in a protected, full-sun border; can also be grown under glass for cut-flower production as it historically was.

directions: Niphetos was once a staple cut-flower rose, prized for its long, pointed buds that open to pure white, loosely double blooms with a light tea fragrance. The lax, somewhat sprawling growth habit benefits from light staking or being tucked among sturdier companions. It flowers repeatedly through the warm season and holds up well to Gulf Coast heat and humidity, though petals can spot in heavy rain. Light, frequent pruning encourages the long stems that made it famous for corsages.

planting.note: Give full sun and room to grow into a large rounded shrub.

directions: Madame Lombard forms a vigorous, well-rounded bush covered in large, full, carmine-pink blooms shaded with salmon and yellow at the base, carried on strong stems. Like other tea roses it thrives in the long hot summers of the Deep South and keeps blooming through conditions that stall modern hybrid teas. Give it room to reach full size and avoid overcrowding to maintain good airflow. Light, regular deadheading and a spring feeding keep flushes coming through fall.

planting.note: Tolerant of poor, sandy soils; useful as an informal hedge or seaside planting.

directions: Belle Poitevine carries large, loosely double, mauve-pink blooms with a strong clove-like fragrance against the typically crinkled, disease-resistant rugosa foliage. It blooms repeatedly through the season and sets attractive large orange-red hips in fall, adding a second season of interest. Extremely cold-hardy and tolerant of salt spray, drought, and poor soil, it needs little more than an annual thinning of old canes to stay healthy. Avoid heavy fertilizing, which can reduce hip set and encourage leggy growth.

planting.note: Also sold as 'Dianthiflora'; a hardy, low-maintenance choice for cold-winter borders.

directions: This distinctive rugosa produces clusters of small, blush-pink blooms with fringed, ragged petal edges that resemble a dianthus flower rather than a typical rose. It shares the rugosa class's toughness, shrugging off cold winters, salt exposure, and poor soil while remaining largely free of blackspot and mildew. The lightly fragrant flowers appear in repeated flushes and rarely set the showy hips typical of other rugosas. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing canes in late winter.

planting.note: Needs a large structure such as a pergola or old tree to climb into; blooms mainly in a single strong spring flush.

directions: Claire Jacquier is an exceptionally vigorous rambling noisette, smothering itself each spring in clusters of small, rosette-shaped, apricot-yellow blooms that fade to cream. It is tough and heat-tolerant, well suited to covering large structures, fences, or old trees in southern gardens where space allows its size. Prune only after the spring bloom flush, removing old wood to make way for new canes, since flowering occurs on growth from the previous season. It needs little supplemental water once established and tolerates poor soil.

common_name: Baronne Henriette de Snoy Tea Rose

planting.note: Give full sun and good drainage; grows into a substantial, well-branched shrub.

directions: This tea rose bears large, full, soft pink blooms shaded with warm peach tones at the center and carries a pronounced sweet tea fragrance. It builds into a sturdy, well-rounded shrub that performs reliably through long, humid Gulf Coast summers, continuing to flower in flushes until frost. Routine light pruning after each bloom cycle keeps the shrub shapely, and good air circulation helps minimize blackspot in wet weather. It is generally considered one of the more cold-tolerant tea roses for its class.
